contract.settlement_definition: Ten unregistered series settle on published rankings, ratings, honours or season statistics rather than on a game. AP series settle only on the AP Top 25 on the Associated Press website: the number of distinct teams ever ranked #1 across all polls including Preseason and Final (KXNCAAMBAPCHURN, floor_strike 9), a team's rank in the Final Rankings expected on Apr 6, 2027 (KXNCAAMBAPRANK, KXNCAAMBTOPAPRANK), or a rank of 5 or better in any eligible poll (KXNCAAMBAPANY). KenPom series settle on the KenPom rating list at a stated timestamp (Mar 15, 2027, 12:00pm EST): #1 or top 25. Award series settle on the named award winner and pay 1/N if there are N co-recipients, and resolve No for a player who does not play in the season. Stat-leader series settle on whole-season per-game averages including the postseason, with NCAA minimum qualification thresholds.

rules_evidence.quote: If the same team holds rank #1 in multiple polls throughout the season, it is counted only once.
rules_evidence.establishes: The poll-churn series counts distinct teams ranked #1 over every AP poll including the Preseason and Final polls, so it is a count of unique holders, not of changes in the top spot.

rules_evidence.quote: Resolution is determined solely by the AP Top 25 Men's College Basketball Polls on the official Associated Press website.
rules_evidence.establishes: The AP website designation (including week labels) is the sole source of truth; other sites showing different week labels do not count.

rules_evidence.quote: Resolution is determined solely by the KenPom ratings on Mar 15, 2027 at 12:00pm EST.
rules_evidence.establishes: The KenPom contract is a snapshot of a computed rating list at a fixed timestamp, so only games and rating updates before that instant matter.

rules_evidence.quote: If multiple recipients are awarded, Yes positions will pay $1/N (rounded down to the nearest cent), where N is the number of awarded recipients
rules_evidence.establishes: A shared award splits the payout, so the expected payout of a candidate depends on the probability of co-winners as well as of winning.

rules_evidence.quote: This market uses statistics for the entire 2026-27 season, including the postseason.
rules_evidence.establishes: Stat-leader contracts include conference-tournament, NCAA and other postseason games, so a deep tournament run adds games to a player's average.

variants_and_edge_cases: Poll churn counts every poll in the season (Preseason through Final), so the number of polls (about 19 to 20) is the number of opportunities for a new #1; a team that is #1 in the preseason counts as soon as the first poll is released.
KXNCAAMBAPANY (any week, top 5) can resolve YES immediately on the Preseason poll or any weekly poll and cannot revert; it is a running-minimum of rank, with a Final poll as the last opportunity.

Final-ranking series (APRANK, TOPAPRANK) depend on tournament results because the Final poll is released after the title game (expected Apr 6, 2027); the champion is typically voted first or near first, so these are advancement contracts in disguise.

KenPom contracts settle at 12:00pm 'EST' on Mar 15, 2027, a date on which US clocks are on daylight time, so the intended instant (EST versus EDT) is ambiguous; ratings change only when KenPom runs its update, so what matters is which games are already counted.

Award contracts: if a player does not play at all the market resolves No; co-recipients split $1 equally; NCAA Tournament Most Outstanding Player is almost always from the champion, so it is a title contract multiplied by a within-team selection.

Stat-leader series (points per game in the SEC, three-pointers made per game nationally) apply NCAA minimum qualification thresholds that the sampled text does not specify, and count postseason games, so leaders can change after the regular season ends.
contract.settlement_data_source: AP Top 25 on apnews.com for poll series; KenPom ratings (a paid-subscription site) for KenPom series; official award announcements for honours; NCAA statistics for stat leaders. The KenPom source is paywalled, so the settled value cannot be independently checked by non-subscribers.

mechanism.summary: Four different data-generating processes are mixed under this key. Poll series are a human aggregation of results: about 60 voters rank 25 teams each week, a team's rank moves with its results, the quality of opponent, and voter inertia, so the distinct-#1 count is a path-dependent Markov process in which each week the current #1 loses with a small probability and a successor is chosen from the contenders. KenPom series are a deterministic computation on game results (opponent-adjusted efficiency margin), so the only uncertainty is future results before the timestamp and the small gap between teams near the cutoff. Award series are two-stage: team success (for the tournament honour) or voting narratives (for player of the year) determines the candidate set, and a within-team or within-set selection picks the winner, with a split-payout rule for co-winners. Stat-leader series are the maximum of many noisy per-game averages across a season, with availability, minimum thresholds and postseason games deciding the winner.

stages.name: Game results of top teams as the shock process
stages.description: Everything in the poll and rating series is downstream of game results of the highest-ranked teams: the weekly chance that the #1 team loses is roughly one minus the win probability in about 1.5 games per week, higher in conference play against ranked teams and road games. A single-game loss probability of 8 to 15 percent for #1 means about one loss every 5 to 8 weeks, so over the roughly 19 polls several changes at #1 are plausible, and the count of distinct holders is a function of both loss frequency and who replaces the loser.
stages.distribution: Bernoulli loss events per week with probabilities from the rating gap and venue; rare but compounding over 19 polls; positively correlated across top teams through shared schedule strength.

stages.name: Voter aggregation and succession at the top
stages.description: Each weekly AP poll is the points total of about 60 individual ballots; voters update ballots after results with inertia (a team usually falls fewer places for a close loss to a strong opponent than for a loss to an unranked team) and some voters prefer unbeaten or recently strong teams. When #1 loses, the successor is typically the highest-ranked team that has not lost recently, but the poll often elevates a new team rather than a previously ranked #1, which is what adds to the distinct count. The per-voter ballots are published by the AP, which enables a voter-level model.
stages.distribution: Aggregate points are a sum of voter-specific ranks with positive correlation between voters; probability that a given team becomes the new #1 follows a softmax over contenders by recent results, rating and prior rank.

stages.name: Final poll after the tournament
stages.description: The Final Rankings are published after the title game and mainly reorder teams by tournament outcome: the champion is typically first or close to it, the runner-up and Final Four teams follow, early exits drop, and teams that missed the tournament fall further. A rank threshold such as top 10 is therefore an advancement contract (reaching the Elite Eight or Final Four) layered on pre-tournament rank, and a specific position such as #3 depends on the order among Final Four teams.
stages.distribution: Rank is an ordinal function of round reached and pre-tournament rank with noise of about 1 to 2 places; probability of a given rank is bell-shaped around the expected rank.

stages.name: KenPom as a deterministic rating list at a timestamp
stages.description: KenPom's rank is a computation on completed games: adjusted offence and defence from all results with opponent and venue adjustments and recency weights, so for a given set of results the rank is determined. Uncertainty comes from the remaining games before March 15 (conference tournaments through Selection Sunday) and from rating updates the next day; near the top, gaps between the first and second team are often below one point of adjusted margin, and near the 25th place the gap between adjacent teams is a fraction of a point, so probabilities are controlled by how many teams sit within an update's noise of the threshold.
stages.distribution: Rating is approximately Gaussian with sd 0.5 to 1.0 points of AdjEM from remaining results; rank thresholds create step events with large probability changes for teams within 1 point of the cutoff.

stages.name: Player awards: selection of a winner from a candidate set
stages.description: For the NCAA Tournament Most Outstanding Player the candidate set is the Final Four and the winner is nearly always from the champion, so probability is the team's title probability times the player's selection share on that team (driven by scoring in the Final Four games and star status). For conference awards such as Defensive Player of the Year the candidate set is the conference's players and voters weigh defensive statistics, team success and narrative. Co-winners split payout.
stages.distribution: Multinomial selection with strong dependence on team success; within the champion, selection share is concentrated (the top player typically holds 40 to 70 percent); co-recipient probability is small but nonzero.

stages.name: Stat leaders: the maximum of noisy season averages
stages.description: A stat-leader contract is true only if a player's final per-game average (including postseason games) tops all qualified players. The leader is a selected maximum: players with the highest current averages are partly lucky, and their expected final average regresses; availability (injuries, DNP), role stability, the qualifying minimum and the number of postseason games a team plays matter. Three-pointers made per game and points per game have different noise levels.
stages.distribution: Maximum of many correlated noisy estimates; winner's curse bias in naive leaders; the leader's identity changes with schedule length and postseason depth.

cbb.number_one_transition_model.label: Markov model of the #1 holder and successor distribution after a loss
cbb.number_one_transition_model.mechanism: The distinct-#1 count is 1 plus the number of changes at the top in which the new holder has not been #1 before; changes occur when the current #1 loses (or is leapfrogged) and the successor is drawn from the contenders.
cbb.number_one_transition_model.rationale: A threshold such as 9 distinct #1 teams is far into the tail of a process whose typical value is 3 to 6 (to be computed from AP archives, not asserted), so the tail depends on the weekly leapfrog probability and on how often the successor is a new team; neither is a function of ratings alone.
cbb.number_one_transition_model.measurement: State: current #1, set of previous #1s, week t (1 to 19). Transition: P(change in week t) = 1 - (1 - L_t) where L_t = prob #1 loses in the week plus P(leapfrog without a loss) estimated from AP archives 2000 to 2026 (leapfrog rate about 3 to 8 percent per week, to be fitted); successor chosen by softmax over the top-8 contenders with features (poll points gap, record, rating gap, unbeaten flag) fitted on past changes; count distinct holders via Monte Carlo of 20,000 seasons using game-by-game loss probabilities from the ratings of the top teams; as-of: latest poll and schedule.
free_sources: AP poll archive (apnews.com / Sports-Reference AP poll history)
raw_data: weekly AP poll top 8 with points
cbb.number_one_transition_model.why: Defines the path-dependent count that the single-game upset variance input does not.

cbb.ap_voter_ballot_panel.label: AP voter ballot panel: individual ballots and update rules
cbb.ap_voter_ballot_panel.mechanism: The AP poll aggregates individual ballots published by voter; each voter's update after results has its own inertia and preferences, so the aggregate response to a loss is the sum of heterogeneous responses.
cbb.ap_voter_ballot_panel.rationale: A voter-level model captures both the average reaction to a loss and the dispersion that makes top-two ties or leapfrogs likely; aggregate-only models cannot tell whether a swing is a few extreme voters or broad movement.
cbb.ap_voter_ballot_panel.measurement: Collect each weekly ballot (voter id, ranks 1 to 25); for each voter-team-week compute rank change as a function of the team's result (win/loss, opponent rank, margin, site), prior rank and a voter fixed effect; fit a mixed model with voter random slopes using 5 seasons; simulate the poll as the sum of voter points from the fitted update rules (25 points for 1st down to 1 for 25th); as-of: previous poll plus results.
free_sources: AP Top 25 voter ballots published on apnews.com (SOURCE_UNVERIFIED for archive depth and bulk access)
cbb.ap_voter_ballot_panel.why: Allows a mechanical simulation of poll movement; the existing voter-behaviour input is a label without data or measurement.

cbb.final_ap_rank_mapping.label: Mapping from tournament outcome and pre-tournament rank to final AP rank
cbb.final_ap_rank_mapping.mechanism: The Final poll orders teams by tournament success first and pre-tournament rank second, with the champion typically placed first or near first.
cbb.final_ap_rank_mapping.rationale: A final-rank contract equals the probability of a bracket outcome mapped through the ordering rule; without the mapping, a top 10 contract would be priced as a rank persistence question, which is wrong because many pre-tournament top-10 teams lose early and fall out.
cbb.final_ap_rank_mapping.measurement: From 2000 to 2026 regress final AP rank on round reached (champion, runner-up, Final Four, Elite Eight, Sweet 16, earlier, missed tournament), pre-tournament AP rank, seed and margin of last game with an ordinal model; output P(final rank = k | round reached, pre rank) with noise sd about 1.5 places; combine with bracket_sim round-reached probabilities by Monte Carlo; as-of: bracket release, updated per round.
free_sources: Sports-Reference AP final polls and tournament results
cbb.final_ap_rank_mapping.why: Converts the bracket simulation into the final-rank distribution that two sampled series settle on.

cbb.kenpom_rank_projection.label: Replication and projection of KenPom ratings to a timestamp
cbb.kenpom_rank_projection.mechanism: KenPom's rating is an opponent-adjusted efficiency margin computed from all completed games with venue and recency treatment, so the rank at a future time is a function of the results that will be counted before that time.
cbb.kenpom_rank_projection.rationale: KXNCAAMBKENPOMRANK and KXNCAAMBKENPOMTOP settle on a snapshot list; the uncertainty is the future results and the rating algorithm, not human opinion, so a faithful replication (with game-by-game updates) is the only way to evaluate crowded ranks.
cbb.kenpom_rank_projection.measurement: Compute AdjO, AdjD and tempo by iterating opponent adjustment to convergence on all D1 games with venue factor 1.4 percent per side (approximate) and a decay weighting by game recency, calibrated so replicated AdjEM matches the KenPom value on historical snapshots with RMSE below 0.3 points; project to Mar 15 12:00 by simulating each remaining game (including conference tournaments) with the pairwise win and margin model, re-running the adjustment per simulated day, and recording rank distributions; as-of: simulation start date, cutoff time of the timestamp.
raw_data: all D1 game results with venue
remaining schedule with conference tournament brackets
cbb.kenpom_rank_projection.why: Targets the specific computed object the series settle on rather than a generic rating ensemble.

cbb.award_selection_model.label: Award selection model: candidate sets, team success dependence and co-recipient probability
cbb.award_selection_model.mechanism: Award winners come from a candidate set defined by performance and team success; the Most Outstanding Player depends on the champion, while Player of the Year awards weigh production, team rank and narrative.
cbb.award_selection_model.rationale: Three contract families (tournament MOP, national player of the year, conference awards) have different drivers; treating them all as 'production' misses that MOP is mostly a title contract, and a 1/N split changes the expected payout.
cbb.award_selection_model.measurement: For MOP: P(player) = sum over teams of P(team champion) * share_player|champion, where share is a multinomial logit on Final Four box-score points per game and star flags fitted to 1990 to 2026 MOP history (champion-conditioned) plus a 3 to 6 percent chance MOP comes from a non-champion; for POY and conference awards: multinomial logit among candidates on BPM, points per game, team rank and conference record, with year-specific fixed effects; co-recipient rate from history (about 1 to 3 percent for major awards); expected payout = P(win) * E[1/N]; as-of: vote deadline and latest stats.
raw_data: player season statistics and team rank at vote time
cbb.award_selection_model.why: Gives a candidate-level probability model per award type; the existing player_usage input is a statistic, not a selection process.

cbb.stat_leader_race_model.label: Leaderboard race model for per-game statistic leaders with postseason games and thresholds
cbb.stat_leader_race_model.mechanism: The leader is the maximum of many noisy per-game averages; future games (including postseason) add samples, injuries remove candidates and thresholds filter qualifiers.
cbb.stat_leader_race_model.rationale: Current leaders are biased upward by luck, so naive extrapolation overstates their chance; the probability that a given player ends first depends on current gap, remaining games (about 8 to 12 for a team after the point of pricing), per-game sd and the probability of missing games.
cbb.stat_leader_race_model.measurement: For each candidate (top 30 by current average, qualified or near-qualified): posterior of true per-game mean mu_i with shrinkage n/(n+15 games) toward a role prior; per-game sd s_i from game logs; remaining games G_i = scheduled regular season games + P(conference tournament games) + expected NCAA/NIT games from bracket_sim; availability probability a_i per game; simulate final average = (sum so far + sum future)/(games played) for 20,000 seasons applying the NCAA minimum threshold rule for qualification; P(leader) = frequency of max; as-of: stats through prior game.
free_sources: Sports-Reference player season and game logs
raw_data: current per-game averages and game logs
cbb.stat_leader_race_model.why: Derives the leader probability from the full structure instead of extrapolating the current top of the list.

cbb.poll_calendar_and_protocol.label: AP poll calendar and designation rules (number of polls, Preseason and Final labels, release timing)
cbb.poll_calendar_and_protocol.mechanism: The number of opportunities for a change at #1 or for a team to enter the top 5 equals the number of polls, and which poll counts as 'Final' is the AP's designation.
cbb.poll_calendar_and_protocol.rationale: Settlement rules count every poll including Preseason and Final and rely on the AP's own labels; a missed week, an early holiday poll or a shifted Final release date changes the count and the resolution timing.
cbb.poll_calendar_and_protocol.measurement: Maintain per season: dates of Preseason, each weekly poll, and Final; number of polls N_polls; AP's 'expected release' date for the Final poll (Apr 6, 2027 expected); poll week labels; indicator for the year-specific schedule; used as the horizon in the transition model and the any-week model; as-of: AP schedule publication.
raw_data: poll release dates and labels by season
cbb.poll_calendar_and_protocol.why: Specifies the horizon and the labels the contracts use.

cbb.ratings.reason: Team strength drives game results and thereby polls and KenPom; but for KenPom contracts the specific KenPom computation matters more than a generic ensemble.

cbb.poll_voter_behavior.reason: Poll movement is a behavioural process and this is the key input, but as stated it is a label; it needs ballot-level data and a fitted update rule.

cbb.resume_metrics.reason: Voters respond to resume (quality wins, losses) beyond efficiency; moderate effect, but better measured by the observed ballot response than by committee metrics.

cbb.conf_strength.reason: Conference strength shades voters' perception of results; effect is small and mostly absorbed by opponent rank.

cbb.sos_remaining.reason: Schedule of ranked-versus-ranked games determines the weekly loss probability; relevant mainly for the top teams.

cbb.single_game_variance.reason: Style-based variance sets loss probabilities for the top team; needed but modest effect relative to rating gap.

cbb.rating_uncertainty.reason: Posterior sd of ratings matters for crowded ranks (KenPom #1) and for the identity of contenders; the replication model needs it.

cbb.player_usage.reason: A rate statistic is only a rough proxy for award candidacy; award selection depends on team success, narrative and counting stats, none of which the usage rate captures.

cbb.news.reason: Injury and eligibility news remove award candidates and teams from contention and change DNP resolution; real but sporadic information.

interactions.mechanism: The drop in poll rank after a loss depends on who the opponent was and where the game was played: a road loss to a top-15 team moves a #1 team down a few places, while a home loss to an unranked team can drop it five or more; the same rating gap implies different poll movement depending on opponent rank and site.
interactions.how_to_test: Regress rank change after a loss on opponent AP rank, site, margin and prior rank using 10 seasons of AP polls and test the opponent-rank by site interaction.

interactions.mechanism: The distinct-#1 count is far into the tail for strikes like 9, where the probability depends strongly and convexly on the per-week change probability: a rise in weekly change probability from 15 to 20 percent multiplies the probability of 9 or more holders several times because it requires many successive changes with new successors.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate the Markov count under change probabilities from 10 to 25 percent and compare the implied P(>=9) to the empirical distribution of distinct #1 counts over 25 seasons.

interactions.mechanism: For rank-based events the relevant statistic is the number of teams within the update noise of the cutoff: the #1 probability is high only if the gap to the next team exceeds about one sd of the rating's projected change, and the top-25 probability for a team at rank 24 to 28 flips sharply as the sd of projected rating changes widens.
interactions.how_to_test: Compute rank probabilities from the simulation for teams at ranks 1 to 3 and 23 to 28 under different sd assumptions and compare with historical changes between early March and Mar 15.

interactions.mechanism: The probability a named player wins Tournament MOP is the product of his team's probability of winning the title and his share of the vote within a champion; because the first factor is small for most teams (a fraction of a percent) and the second is concentrated in the top player, the product is extremely skewed toward stars on top seeds.
interactions.how_to_test: Compare predicted MOP probabilities from the product model against historical MOP team and player identities, including the non-champion exceptions.

interactions.mechanism: The leaders for points per game and three-pointers made are determined jointly by usage (shot volume) and by a few players' minutes and availability; high-volume shooters have high mean but also large sd and higher injury exposure, so the leader probability depends on the joint of mean, sd and games played, not on the mean alone.
interactions.how_to_test: Simulate leader probability for the current top-10 candidates with and without game-level sd and availability and compare to history of mid-season versus final leaders.

nonlinearities.shape: asymmetric: rank loss after a defeat exceeds the rank gain after an equivalent win, and the drop is larger at the top of the poll
nonlinearities.why: Voters treat the #1 team's loss as more informative than a win and a #1 team that loses to an unranked opponent can fall many places, so rank movement is not linear in margin or rating gap and the top spot is fragile.

nonlinearities.shape: sigmoid in rating gap over projected rating sd for rank-based events
nonlinearities.why: P(#1 on KenPom) moves from near 0 to near 1 over a gap of a few sds of projected change; with a gap of 1 point and sd of 0.7 the probability is only about 90 percent, far from the near-certainty a point estimate implies.

nonlinearities.shape: convex effect on tail counts of distinct #1 teams
nonlinearities.why: Because the probability of nine or more holders needs repeated losses with new successors, a small rise in single-game upset variance causes a disproportionately large rise in the tail probability.
